en: The *Buddhabhāṣita-aguruvarga-sūtra*.
According to Sengyou’s catalogue, this is an ancient scripture from the period of Master Dao’an; it is now appended to the Han Records.
Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park. The Buddha...
He addressed the bhikṣus, saying:
"In the past, there was a merchant named Ajiravatī who lived in great wealth, possessing gold, silver, rare treasures, and a vast number of servants and slaves."
Ajita did not believe in rebirth in future lives, nor that performing good deeds results in good, or that performing evil deeds results in evil. Ajita said:
"When a person dies, their body becomes external earth; the body's water becomes external water; the body's fire becomes external fire; and the body's wind becomes external wind."
The body is entirely a composite; once a person has died, they will never be born again.
Whatever good or evil a person has done—what the mind has conceived, what the mouth has spoken, and what the body has performed—all must be cast away, for after this, one is not born again.

At that time, Ajita took several tens of millions in wealth and set out together with five hundred merchants; Ajita was the most honorable and eminent among the traveling merchants who accompanied him.

When traveling through a region where there was neither water nor grass, the food, fodder, and water they carried were all exhausted; after traveling for one day and two days, they saw no water or grass, and after traveling for three and four days, they still saw no water or grass.
The merchants were all struck with terror and said,
"Are we all now destined to starve to death here in this desolate wilderness!
Each of them wept aloud, calling out for their parents, wives, and children.
Ajātaśatru dispatched four riders to spread out and search for water and grass.

Ajātaśatru himself went on ahead and from afar saw a tree; its leaves were lush green and its fruits and gourds grew in profusion. He thought to himself, "There must surely be water beneath this tree," and so he proceeded toward it.
He saw a man of incomparable beauty; seeing Āgñāta-Kauṇḍinya approaching on horseback from afar, he went out to meet him and said, "Welcome!
Please tell me what you seek."
When Ajvulu saw the person under the tree answer him, he was greatly delighted, as if he had been reborn.
The person under the tree asked:
"From where have you come?"
"Where do you wish to go? Ajita replied,
"I seek to save my own life and the lives of five hundred people and animals."
The person under the tree asked:
"What do you seek? He replied:

"I wish for water. The man beneath the tree then raised his right hand, and water issued from the tips of his five fingers like a flowing spring; it was exceedingly fragrant and delicious. He said to Ajñāta-kaundinya, "Drink as much as you desire."
Having drunk, he again asked for food. The man beneath the tree then raised his right hand, and delicious food issued forth from the tips of his fingers.
Once Ajvulu had eaten his fill, he raised his voice and wept bitterly.
A person under the tree asked:
"Virtuous one! Why do you weep?"

Aṅgulimāla said: "Our company of five hundred men and their beasts have not received food or drink for three or four days. We are at the extreme limit of hunger, our lives hanging by a thread; that is why I am weeping!"
The man under the tree said to Ajita,
"If you bring five hundred men and their livestock, I shall provide enough food for all of them.
Ajita immediately set out at a gallop and called his companions, saying to them:
"Do not worry any longer!
You have already found a place for food and drink; follow me as we go.
The companions were greatly delighted and followed him to the foot of the tree, where they all joined their palms in reverence and paid homage to the person beneath the tree.
A person under the tree asked,
"What do you wish to obtain?
and everyone replied:
“We are greatly hungry and thirsty.
The man under the tree immediately raised his right hand with its five fingers extended, and forthwith great water issued forth like flowing springs; men, horses, and livestock all drank from it.

When they again asked for food, the man under the tree once more raised his right hand with its five fingers extended, and produced exquisite food and drink to give them, so that the five hundred people and the animals were all fully satisfied.
The man beneath the tree then asked the five hundred people:
"What do you all seek to attain?
The merchants replied:
"We all wish to reach the great ocean to seek out precious treasures.
The man beneath the tree then asked,
"Since you all wish to seek out precious treasures, they may now emerge from my hand."

The person beneath the tree then raised his right hand, and from the tips of his five fingers there emerged gold, silver, crystal, lapis lazuli, coral, amber, and white pearls. The person then gathered them up; as he took each, it became as heavy as if it had been removed.
The man under the tree said to Ajita:

"Take this gold and silver back to your hometown and use it to give alms to the poor; to those who wish for food, give them food; to those who wish for gold, silver, wealth, or clothing, give them as much as they desire."

"May you all, O practitioners of the Way, offer prayers for me, so that I may obtain this merit; may wonderful things emerge from my hands, and may you also cause me to escape quickly from this desolate wilderness."
Upon hearing these words, Ajvulu was greatly alarmed and terrified; he then prostrated himself with his head to the ground and asked, "Virtuous one, who are you?
Are you a deva?"
Is it a dragon?
A ghost or spirit?
Or a human being?
The person under the tree said:
"I am neither a deva, nor a nāga, nor a yakṣa, nor a human; I am a powerful preta."

In a previous life, I was extremely poor in this kingdom and used to sit constantly beneath the city gate. Although I was destitute, my mind was pure and clean, and I cherished the śramaṇas and practitioners of the Way. Being poor myself, I could not give to others; however, when I saw others practicing giving, I rejoiced on their behalf.
At that time, when Kāśyapa Buddha had entered parinirvāṇa, various bhikṣus came to beg for food from me, and I replied to those bhikṣus: "I have nothing."
I merely pointed out from afar within the city that at such-and-such a house one could obtain food, while at such-and-such a house one could not.
When the bhikṣu came out after begging and I saw that he had obtained something, I was immediately filled with joy.
Furthermore, when Kāśyapa Buddha entered parinirvāṇa, there was a king named Ki-li who erected a stūpa made of the seven treasures for Kāśyapa Buddha. I immediately placed my hand upon it and said:
"May I obtain its merit."
"When the King offered excellent items to the Buddha’s stupa, I would immediately take them in my hand and say:
'May I obtain the merit thereof.
However, because of poverty, I have never observed the fast; I ate at irregular hours and drank alcohol. For this reason, after death, I have become a wealthy *pūtana* spirit."
It is because in my previous lives I saw others performing good deeds and felt joy on their behalf, placing my hand upon their possessions; for this reason, five fingers have emerged from my palms.
It is because during my lifetime I never observed the fasts that I have become a *pūtana* ghost such as this.
Ajita thought to himself:
"Previously, I did not believe in rebirth in future lives, nor that performing good deeds would result in good retribution, nor that performing evil deeds would result in evil retribution."

Now, with my own eyes I have seen that there is indeed a future life, and that one who performs good deeds will certainly experience good results, while one who performs evil deeds will certainly experience evil results.

From this day forward, when I return to my hometown, I shall diligently perform good deeds and practice giving to others, granting whatever they seek. Should anyone desire gold, silver, precious gems, food and drink, or clothing and bedding, I shall give it all to them and never refuse anyone.
Āgullu returned to his home village and said to the people of the country:
"Whoever desires gold, silver, precious gems, clothing, bedding, food, or drink, let them seek out whatever they wish; all may come and take it."

In this manner, his giving was immeasurable; every day he provided meals for eighty-four thousand practitioners of the Way, such that the overflowing water flowed out through the gate until people had to use boats to cross it.

Agnidatta performed virtuous deeds with the utmost sincerity; after his death, he ascended to the second heaven, the Trāyastriṃśa, where he became a celestial being residing four hundred and eighty *li* away from the throne of Śakra, Lord of Devas.
"In that country, there was a female beggar named Tse who, with a virtuous mind, took a bowl of rice gruel and gave it to the śramaṇa Mahākāśyapa."
After death, this woman was also reborn in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven as a celestial being, occupying the third seat beside Śakra Devendra, surpassing the other devas in five respects.
What are the five matters?
First, long life; second, physical beauty; [and so forth].
Third, peace and happiness;
fourth, wisdom; fifth, majestic spiritual power.
He was superior to the other devas.
Later, when the Buddha’s mother suddenly passed away, she was reborn in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven; at that time, the Buddha preached the sūtras for his mother in the heavens.
Having finished preaching the sūtras, the Buddha’s mother and countless other devas all attained the stage of Srotāpanna.
The Buddha saw that because Aṅgīrasa had given alms to others, he sat four hundred and eighty *li* away from Śakra, Lord of Devas;
yet he also saw a woman begging for alms who gave rice gruel to the śramaṇa Mahākāśyapa, and that she occupied the third seat beside Śakra, Lord of Devas, surpassing the other devas in five respects.
The Buddha saw them all and recognized them; he immediately called out to Ajīvaka from afar, saying:
"O virtuous man who practices giving!
Come and meet me."
Ajñāta-kaundinya immediately came forward, placed his head upon the ground in prostration before the Buddha, and addressed the Buddha, saying:

"I have given much in alms to the great assembly, yet I have obtained only the status of an ordinary person; I have not attained the stage of Srotāpanna, Sakṛdāgāmin, Anāgāmin, Arhat, Pratyekabuddha, or the Way of the Buddha."
Now, seeing this beggar woman who offered rice gruel to the śramaṇa Mahākāśyapa, she occupies the third seat beside Śakra in the present world, surpassing the other devas in five matters.
"If a person gives even a small object to Mahākāśyapa and obtains such merit as this, it is for this reason that he has personally attained such great wealth and nobility.
Having spoken thus, the deva paid homage to the Buddha and departed.
The Sūtra Spoken by the Buddha on Ajvulu (Ajiravatī)
